AI SDR platforms

Built for outbound at volume and enterprise contracts — one raised $74M on that thesis. They generate pipeline; they don't answer the inquiry already sitting in your inbox.

Client-management suites

HoneyBook, Dubsado and Moxie run $12–$129 a month and handle proposals, contracts and invoices. All of it happens after someone replies.

The gap

A three-person consultancy can't hire an SDR and won't buy enterprise software. They lose deals to silence — while they're in a client meeting. That's the seat Relay takes.

HOW IT WORKS

Three steps, one hard rule.

1

It reads

Every inbound message is parsed for budget, timeline, service line and intent — then checked against the minimum project size you set.

2

It drafts

A reply in your tone that names their goal, handles the budget question honestly, asks your qualifying questions, and offers two times you actually have free.

3

You approve

Nothing sends on its own. The draft waits in your queue, you edit a line if you want, and you press send.

The hard rule: a client's email is data, never an instruction. Relay reads what they wrote; it never does what a message tells it to do. That's what makes an approval gate worth having.
THE MARKET

50,025 firms in one US category alone — and 84% of them have fewer than five people.

Who pays

Solo consultants and micro-agencies already spending $12–$129 a month on client tooling that doesn't respond for them. Relay slots into a budget line that exists.

Why now

Drafting a competent, context-aware reply became cheap and good enough in the last eighteen months. The approval gate makes it safe to sell to people whose reputation is the product.

Where it grows

Answer first, then own the relationship: proposals, follow-up cadence, scheduling, renewals. The inbox is the wedge, not the ceiling.

HONEST STATUS

What works today, and what's next.

Working in the prototype

  • Inbound message parsing — budget, timeline, service, intent, fit
  • Draft generation in three configurable tones
  • Real availability lookup and conflict-checked booking
  • Calendar file (.ics) export and mail-client handoff
  • Pipeline stages, analytics and follow-up queue
  • The revenue model, editable with your own numbers

Next build steps

  • Model-backed drafting behind the same approval gate
  • Gmail and Outlook OAuth for real inbound and sending
  • Google / Microsoft calendar sync
  • Accounts, workspaces and billing
  • Background follow-up scheduling

Plain about the boundaries: the drafting engine in this prototype is deterministic rules running in your browser, not a live model. Client data is fictional. Nothing is emailed, no calendar is connected, and changes save only to your own browser. The architecture is built so that one function gets swapped for a model call — the approval gate, the parsing contract and the UI stay exactly as they are.
